slides: Now let's look at the three types of trial and error.

slides.say: Trial and error comes in three types, and each type gets its own lesson, with questions.
Type one is general problems. Nothing in the question tells us what to try first. So we just try, like we did with the pens and the notebooks.

Type two is minimum and maximum. Here a little understanding tells us which way to push, so we need fewer tries. For example, three friends share ten sweets, and each gets at least one. What's the most one friend can get? To make one share as big as possible, we give the others as little as possible, one each. So the most is ten minus two, which is eight.
at: Type two is minimum and maximum
So the most is ten minus two

slides.say: The same push with other numbers. Five friends share twenty sweets. The other four get one each, that's four. So the most one friend can get is twenty minus four, sixteen.
at: The other four get one each

slides.say: Type three is patterns. A rule repeats again and again, and we write the items one by one. For example, a number starts at three and doubles each time. Three, six, twelve, twenty-four. So the fourth number is twenty-four.
Another rule. Start at twenty and take away three each time. Twenty, seventeen, fourteen, eleven. Here we hardly think and hardly make mistakes. It's mostly trial, and very little error.
at: Start at twenty and take away three

slides.say: One reminder from the first topic, because many of these questions ask it. Three words decide the question. Must, could and cannot.
Two positive whole numbers add up to fourteen. Could one of them be three? Yes. Three plus eleven is fourteen. For could, one example that works is enough.
Must one of them be odd? Three and eleven are both odd. But two and twelve also add up to fourteen, and both are even. So one allowed example fails, and must is out.
at: two and twelve also add up

slides.say: Must one of them be at least seven? Here no example can prove it, we need a reason. If both were six or less, the sum would be at most six plus six, twelve. That's less than fourteen. So yes, one of them is always at least seven.
at: If both were six or less

slides.say: And cannot means it never works, for any allowed numbers. Can both be bigger than seven? No. The smallest whole numbers bigger than seven are eight and eight, and that's already sixteen. So could needs one example, must needs every case, and cannot means no case at all.
at: Can both be bigger than seven

slides.say: Every question in this chapter comes before its video. So try it on paper first. Stuck? Write what you do know, the first try or two. Then watch the video, and compare.

slides: Let's start with type one. [pause] I'll see you in the next video.
